The last person known to catch smallpox naturally was Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook and health worker in Merca, Somalia, who fell ill in October 1977. He recovered. In 1979 experts certified the disease gone, and in May 1980 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared it eradicated. It is still the only human disease ever wiped out.

Smallpox had killed people for thousands of years. It struck the Aztecs in 1520 and killed hundreds of millions in the 1900s alone. Edward Jenner's vaccine of 1796 gave the means to stop it, but it took a world campaign. WHO began its intensified eradication programme in 1967. Instead of vaccinating everyone, teams hunted down each case and vaccinated everyone around it, a method called ring vaccination.

By the mid-1970s the last cases were in South Asia and the Horn of Africa. Maalin caught the mild form, variola minor, after briefly guiding a car that carried two sick children to an isolation camp. He had avoided vaccination. Health workers traced and vaccinated his contacts, and none of them fell ill.

The very last death from smallpox came in 1978, from a laboratory leak in Birmingham, England. Maalin later worked on the campaign against polio in Somalia, and died of malaria in 2013 while doing that work.
